question: What is the main goal of building a safety culture in a hospital?

options.A: Eliminating the need for personal protective equipment
options.B: Punishing staff members who make clinical errors
options.C: Encouraging staff to report mistakes so processes can be fixed
options.D: Reducing staff workload during busy shift hours

explanation: A great safety culture means staff feel safe reporting mistakes. That way, we fix the broken system instead of just blaming the person! [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why is keeping nurses safe just as important as keeping patients safe?

options.A: Hospital management is legally required to pay hazard allowances
options.B: Patients refuse treatment from nurses who look tired or stressed
options.C: Injured nurses are immediately transferred to administrative duties
options.D: Protected nurses are able to provide better, continuous care to patients

explanation: When nurses stay safe, healthy, and injury-free, they can be right there on the ward providing the best care for their patients. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h1)

question: What should you do immediately if you notice a frayed electrical cord on an infusion pump?

options.A: Report the issue during the next month's departmental meeting
options.B: Use the pump only when plugged into a backup generator
options.C: Wrap the frayed section securely with adhesive plaster
options.D: Remove the equipment from service and tag it as faulty

explanation: Never ignore damaged wires! Take the device out of use right away and label it as faulty to prevent shock or fire hazards. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h2)

question: Which environmental hazard causes the most night-time falls among elderly patients in the ward?

options.A: High noise levels from ward corridors
options.B: Dimly lit pathways to the bathroom
options.C: Firm mattresses on standard hospital beds
options.D: Low room temperatures during the night

explanation: When the lights are dim, patients can easily trip over things on their way to the bathroom in the dark. Good lighting is key! [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in a hospital?

options.B: Wearing sterile gowns at all times
options.D: Changing bed linens after every shift

explanation: Simple hand hygiene is your superpower! It stops germs from passing between patients and staff faster than anything else. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h3)

question: After giving an injection, what is the safest thing to do with the used needle?

options.A: Place the needle on the bedside tray for later disposal
options.B: Break the needle before dropping it into the trash can
options.C: Dispose of the uncapped needle directly into a safety box
options.D: Recap the needle carefully using a two-handed technique

explanation: Never recap needles! Drop them straight into the safety box (sharps container) uncapped to avoid accidental needle-pricks. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h3)

question: How should you position the bed for a patient who is at high risk of falling?

options.A: Tilted at a 45-degree angle for chest expansion
options.B: At the lowest position with wheels locked
options.C: Free-floating without the wheel locks engaged
options.D: At the highest level for easy nursing access

explanation: Keep the bed low so that if they do roll out, they won't fall far, and lock those wheels so the bed doesn't slide away! [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which type of medication makes hospital patients much more likely to suffer a fall?
explanation: Sedatives make patients drowsy and dizzy, throwing off their balance and increasing their chances of a fall. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h4)

question: Before giving any medication, how many unique patient identifiers must you check?
explanation: Always check at least two things (like name and hospital number) to be 100% sure you are giving the right drug to the right patient. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h5)

question: When is the right time to document that you have given a medication?

options.A: At the end of the entire shift during handover reports
options.B: Whenever time permits later in the afternoon or evening
options.C: Immediately after the patient swallows or receives the drug
options.D: Before drawing up the medication from the vial or ampoule

explanation: Always chart right after giving the drug. Doing it right away prevents accidental double-dosing and keeps records accurate. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h5)

question: Which document tells you how to safely handle and clean up hospital chemicals?
explanation: The Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) is your go-to guide for chemical risks, required protective gear, and spill cleanups. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why do healthcare workers in the radiology department wear personal dosimeter badges?

options.A: To block scattered radiation from entering the respiratory tract
options.B: To identify their specific department during emergency drills
options.C: To prove their professional certification to hospital auditors
options.D: To measure their cumulative exposure to ionizing radiation

explanation: Dosimeter badges track how much radiation a worker absorbs over time, helping to keep exposure safely within legal limits. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h6)

question: In the fire safety acronym RACE, what does the letter 'A' stand for?

options.A: Apply oxygen to the affected room
options.C: Alarm or activate the fire system

explanation: In RACE, 'A' stands for Activate the alarm! Sounding the alarm alerts everyone so the rescue process can begin. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h7)

question: What is the main reason for running regular fire and emergency drills in a hospital?

options.A: To test the speed of the local public fire service
options.B: To identify patients who require physical restraint devices
options.C: To ensure staff respond calmly and correctly during a crisis
options.D: To fulfill mandatory requirements for building insurance policies

explanation: Practice makes perfect! Routine drills help staff stay calm, know the exit routes, and act without panic during a real emergency. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h7)

question: Where should you record the details of an accidental medication error involving a patient?

options.A: In a private notebook kept in the nurse's locker
options.B: On the public ward noticeboard for staff review
options.C: On the front cover of the patient's case note
options.D: On a separate hospital incident report form

explanation: Incident reports go on special hospital forms—separate from patient charts—to help management review and improve safety systems. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h8)

question: Why should you NOT mention the incident report inside the patient's clinical nursing notes?

options.A: Clinical notes are discarded upon the patient's discharge
options.B: Hospital management reviews incident reports before nursing notes
options.C: Nursing notes are meant exclusively for recording financial charges
options.D: It keeps the incident report separate from the legal medical record

explanation: Keeping incident reports out of patient charts protects them as internal quality tools rather than part of everyday legal medical records. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h8)
